Data: Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer (WDBC)

Each row is a patient. Outcome Diagnosis is Benign or Malignant. Predictors are 30 numeric features derived from FNA images.

url_data  <- "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/breast-cancer-wisconsin/wdbc.data"
raw <- read.csv(url_data, header = FALSE)

names(raw) <- c("ID","Diagnosis",
                "radius_mean","texture_mean","perimeter_mean","area_mean","smoothness_mean",
                "compactness_mean","concavity_mean","concave_points_mean","symmetry_mean","fractal_dimension_mean",
                "radius_se","texture_se","perimeter_se","area_se","smoothness_se",
                "compactness_se","concavity_se","concave_points_se","symmetry_se","fractal_dimension_se",
                "radius_worst","texture_worst","perimeter_worst","area_worst","smoothness_worst",
                "compactness_worst","concavity_worst","concave_points_worst","symmetry_worst","fractal_dimension_worst")

bc <- raw %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(Diagnosis = factor(Diagnosis, levels = c("B","M"))) %>%  # B = negative, M = positive
  select(-ID)

Train/test split (stratified):

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(bc, prop = 0.8, strata = Diagnosis)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

nrow(train); nrow(test)
## [1] 454
## [1] 115

A helper to compute the metrics we’ve discussed (AUC is threshold-free; others use a threshold, default 0.5):

eval_metrics <- function(truth, prob_pos, thr = 0.5) {
  truth <- factor(truth, levels = c("B","M"))     # "M" is event
  cls   <- factor(ifelse(prob_pos >= thr, "M","B"), levels = c("B","M"))
  tibble(
    AUC  = roc_auc_vec(truth, prob_pos, event_level = "second"),
    Sens = sens_vec(truth, cls,        event_level = "second"),
    Spec = spec_vec(truth, cls,        event_level = "second"),
    PPV  = ppv_vec (truth, cls,        event_level = "second"),
    NPV  = npv_vec (truth, cls,        event_level = "second"),
    Acc  = accuracy_vec(truth, cls)
  )
}

Part A — Gaussian Naive Bayes (treat all predictors as continuous)

e1071::naiveBayes models numeric predictors with a Gaussian density per class and factors with multinomial/Bernoulli. Here we keep all 30 features numeric → Gaussian NB.

nb_gauss <- naiveBayes(Diagnosis ~ ., data = train, laplace = 0)  # no smoothing needed for continuous
# Posterior probability for Malignant ("M")
p_tr_g <- predict(nb_gauss, newdata = train, type = "raw")[,"M"]
p_te_g <- predict(nb_gauss, newdata = test,  type = "raw")[,"M"]

metrics_gauss <- bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(train$Diagnosis, p_tr_g) %>% mutate(Set = "Train"),
  eval_metrics(test$Diagnosis,  p_te_g) %>% mutate(Set = "Test")
) %>% relocate(Set)

kbl2(metrics_gauss, caption = "Gaussian Naive Bayes: Performance (threshold = 0.5)")

ROC curve (train vs test):

train$estimate = p_tr_g
test$estimate = p_te_g
roc_train_g <- yardstick::roc_curve(data = train, Diagnosis, estimate, event_level = "second") %>% mutate(Set = "Train")
roc_test_g  <- yardstick::roc_curve(data = test, Diagnosis,  estimate, event_level = "second") %>% mutate(Set = "Test")

bind_rows(roc_train_g, roc_test_g) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = 1 - specificity, y = sensitivity, color = Set)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 1) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 3) +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(title = "Gaussian Naive Bayes — ROC", x = "1 - Specificity (FPR)", y = "Sensitivity (TPR)")

Part B — Mixed-Type Naive Bayes (some binary, some multinomial, some continuous)

Here we transform a few predictors to binary (median split) and a few to multinomial (tertiles), and leave the rest continuous. naiveBayes will combine the appropriate likelihoods under the Naive assumption.

Choices for this demo

  • Binary: radius_mean, texture_mean, perimeter_mean (High vs Low, median split)
  • Multinomial (3-level): area_mean, smoothness_mean (Low/Med/High via tertiles)
  • Continuous: all remaining features stay numeric
make_mixed <- function(df) {
  out <- df
  
  # Binary via median split
  for (v in c("radius_mean","texture_mean","perimeter_mean")) {
    med <- median(out[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
    out[[paste0(v,"_bin")]] <- factor(ifelse(out[[v]] > med, "High","Low"))
    out[[v]] <- NULL
  }
  
  # Multinomial via tertiles
  for (v in c("area_mean","smoothness_mean")) {
    qs <- quantile(out[[v]], probs = c(1/3, 2/3), na.rm = TRUE)
    cutv <- cut(out[[v]],
                breaks = c(-Inf, qs[1], qs[2], Inf),
                labels = c("Low","Med","High"),
                right = TRUE)
    out[[paste0(v,"_ter")]] <- factor(cutv)
    out[[v]] <- NULL
  }
  
  out
}

train_mx <- make_mixed(train)
test_mx  <- make_mixed(test)

glimpse(train_mx)

p_tr_mx <- predict(nb_mixed, newdata = train_mx, type = "raw")[,"M"]
p_te_mx <- predict(nb_mixed, newdata = test_mx,  type = "raw")[,"M"]

  eval_metrics(train_mx$Diagnosis, p_tr_mx) %>% mutate(Set = "Train"),
  eval_metrics(test_mx$Diagnosis,  p_te_mx) %>% mutate(Set = "Test")
) %>% relocate(Set)

Optional — Threshold tuning by Youden’s J (for either model)

Pick a threshold on the training set that maximizes Youden’s Index \(J = \text{Sens} + \text{Spec} - 1\), then evaluate on test.

Note: This version is improved over before.

tune_threshold_j <- function(truth, prob, grid = NULL) {
  if(is.null(grid)){grid <- c(0,sort(unique(prob)),1)}
  
  truth <- factor(truth, levels = c("B","M"))
  best_t <- NULL; best_j <- -Inf
  
  for (t in grid) {
    cls <- factor(ifelse(prob >= t, "M","B"), levels = c("B","M"))
    se <- sens_vec(truth, cls, event_level = "second")
    sp <- spec_vec(truth, cls, event_level = "second")
    j  <- as.numeric(se + sp - 1)
    if (!is.na(j) && j >= best_j) { 
      best_t <- c(best_t,t) 
      if(j > best_j){best_t <- t}
      
      best_j <- j 
    }
  }
  sum(range(best_t))/2
}

thr_g <- tune_threshold_j(train$Diagnosis, p_tr_g)
thr_m <- tune_threshold_j(train_mx$Diagnosis, p_tr_mx)

perf_tuned <- bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(train$Diagnosis,    p_tr_g, thr_g) %>% mutate(Model = "Gaussian NB", Set = "Train", Thr = round(thr_g,3)),
  eval_metrics(test$Diagnosis,     p_te_g, thr_g) %>% mutate(Model = "Gaussian NB", Set = "Test",  Thr = round(thr_g,3)),
  eval_metrics(train_mx$Diagnosis, p_tr_mx, thr_m) %>% mutate(Model = "Mixed NB",    Set = "Train", Thr = round(thr_m,3)),
  eval_metrics(test_mx$Diagnosis,  p_te_mx, thr_m) %>% mutate(Model = "Mixed NB",    Set = "Test",  Thr = round(thr_m,3))
) %>% relocate(Model, Set, Thr)

Summary

  • Naive Bayes is a framework: multiply class-conditional likelihoods per feature under conditional independence.
  • With e1071::naiveBayes, numeric variables are modeled as Gaussian; factors are modeled as multinomial/Bernoulli with optional Laplace smoothing.
  • You can mix feature types in the same model (as we did with binary + multinomial + continuous).
  • Report both threshold-free (AUC) and thresholded (Se/Sp/PPV/NPV/Acc) performance; optionally tune the threshold (e.g., Youden’s J) on training and report test-set results.

Part C — Kernel-Density Naive Bayes (non-parametric for continuous features)

Not all of the variables have a normal distribution. For example,

ggplot(data = train) + geom_histogram(aes(radius_mean))

We now replace the Gaussian assumption for continuous variables with kernel density estimates (KDE) per class and per feature. This lets us capture skewness, heavy tails, and multi-modality that a Normal model can’t.

Fit/predict helpers for KDE-NB

# ----- Utilities -----

# Stable log-sum-exp for posterior normalization
logsumexp <- function(z) {
  m <- max(z)
  m + log(sum(exp(z - m)))
}

# Build Laplace-smoothed class-conditional probability tables for factor features
fit_factor_tables <- function(df, y, alpha = 1) {
  lev_y <- levels(y)
  facs  <- names(df)[vapply(df, is.factor, logical(1))]
  out <- vector("list", length(facs)); names(out) <- facs
  for (f in facs) {
    tab <- table(y, df[[f]])
    # Laplace smoothing by row (class)
    tab_sm <- sweep(tab + alpha, 1, rowSums(tab) + alpha * ncol(tab), "/")
    out[[f]] <- as.matrix(tab_sm)[lev_y, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  out
}

# For continuous features: per-class KDE objects + interpolators
fit_kde_tables <- function(df, y, bw = "nrd0", adjust = 1, kernel = "gaussian", gridsize = 512) {
  nums <- names(df)[vapply(df, is.numeric, logical(1))]
  lev_y <- levels(y)
  out <- vector("list", length(nums)); names(out) <- nums
  for (v in nums) {
    dens_list <- vector("list", length(lev_y)); names(dens_list) <- lev_y
    for (k in lev_y) {
      xk <- df[[v]][y == k]
      # Handle degenerate cases: if all equal, jitter slightly
      if (sd(xk, na.rm = TRUE) == 0) {
        xk <- xk + rnorm(length(xk), sd = 1e-8)
      }
      dk <- density(xk, bw = bw, adjust = adjust, kernel = kernel, n = gridsize)
      # Interpolator; rule=2 for constant extrapolation at tails
      fk <- approxfun(dk$x, dk$y, rule = 2)
      dens_list[[k]] <- list(x = dk$x, y = dk$y, f = fk)
    }
    out[[v]] <- dens_list
  }
  out
}

# ----- Model fit -----
naive_bayes_kde_fit <- function(data, yvar = "Diagnosis", alpha = 1,
                                bw = "nrd0", adjust = 1, kernel = "gaussian") {
  y <- factor(data[[yvar]])
  X <- data[, setdiff(names(data), yvar), drop = FALSE]
  priors <- prop.table(table(y))
  fac_tables <- fit_factor_tables(X, y, alpha = alpha)
  kde_tables <- fit_kde_tables(X, y, bw = bw, adjust = adjust, kernel = kernel)
  list(yvar = yvar,
       priors = priors,
       fac_tables = fac_tables,
       kde_tables = kde_tables,
       levels = levels(y),
       num_vars = names(kde_tables),
       fac_vars = names(fac_tables),
       alpha = alpha)
}

# ----- Prediction (posterior for positive class "M") -----
naive_bayes_kde_predict_proba <- function(model, newdata, positive = "M", eps = 1e-12) {
  lev_y <- model$levels
  X <- newdata[, setdiff(names(newdata), model$yvar), drop = FALSE]
  n <- nrow(X)
  log_post <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n, ncol = length(lev_y))
  colnames(log_post) <- lev_y
  # Precompute logs of priors
  log_prior <- log(as.numeric(model$priors)[match(lev_y, names(model$priors))])
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    # For each class, accumulate log-likelihoods
    for (k in seq_along(lev_y)) {
      kk <- lev_y[k]
      lp <- log_prior[k]
      # numeric vars via KDE
      for (v in model$num_vars) {
        if (!is.null(model$kde_tables[[v]][[kk]])) {
          dens_val <- model$kde_tables[[v]][[kk]]$f(X[[v]][i])
          lp <- lp + log(pmax(dens_val, eps))
        }
      }
      # factor vars via Laplace-smoothed tables
      for (f in model$fac_vars) {
        tab <- model$fac_tables[[f]]
        lvl <- as.character(X[[f]][i])
        if (!is.na(lvl) && lvl %in% colnames(tab)) {
          lp <- lp + log(pmax(tab[kk, lvl], eps))
        } else {
          # unseen level → uniform tiny mass
          lp <- lp + log(eps)
        }
      }
      log_post[i, k] <- lp
    }
  }
  # softmax to probabilities
  probs <- t(apply(log_post, 1, function(z) {
    denom <- logsumexp(z)
    exp(z - denom)
  }))
  as.numeric(probs[, match(positive, lev_y)])
}

Build mixed feature set (reuse Part B) and fit KDE-NB

We’ll use the same mixed feature construction as before (binary + multinomial + remaining continuous), but now the continuous features are modeled with KDE instead of Gaussians.

# Reuse make_mixed(train) from Part B
train_kde <- make_mixed(train)
test_kde  <- make_mixed(test)

# Fit KDE-NB (Laplace=1 for categorical features; KDE for numeric)
kde_nb <- naive_bayes_kde_fit(train_kde, yvar = "Diagnosis", alpha = 1,
                              bw = "nrd0", adjust = 1, kernel = "gaussian")

# Posterior P(M | X)
p_tr_kde <- naive_bayes_kde_predict_proba(kde_nb, train_kde)
p_te_kde <- naive_bayes_kde_predict_proba(kde_nb, test_kde)

metrics_kde <- bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(train_kde$Diagnosis, p_tr_kde) %>% mutate(Set = "Train"),
  eval_metrics(test_kde$Diagnosis,  p_te_kde) %>% mutate(Set = "Test")
) %>% relocate(Set)

kbl2(metrics_kde, caption = "Kernel-Density Naive Bayes (mixed features): Performance (threshold = 0.5)")

ROC curves for KDE-NB:

train$estimate_kde = p_tr_kde
test$estimate_kde = p_te_kde
roc_train_kde <- yardstick::roc_curve(data = train, Diagnosis, estimate_kde, event_level = "second") %>% mutate(Set = "Train")
roc_test_kde  <- yardstick::roc_curve(data = test, Diagnosis,  estimate_kde, event_level = "second") %>% mutate(Set = "Test")


bind_rows(roc_train_kde, roc_test_kde) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = 1 - specificity, y = sensitivity, color = Set)) +
  geom_path(size = 1) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 3) +
  coord_equal() + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(title = "KDE-Naive Bayes — ROC", x = "1 - Specificity (FPR)", y = "Sensitivity (TPR)")

(Optional) Tune thresholds by Youden’s J for KDE-NB

thr_kde <- tune_threshold_j(train_kde$Diagnosis, p_tr_kde)

perf_kde_tuned <- bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(train_kde$Diagnosis, p_tr_kde, thr_kde) %>% mutate(Model = "KDE-NB", Set = "Train", Thr = round(thr_kde,3)),
  eval_metrics(test_kde$Diagnosis,  p_te_kde, thr_kde) %>% mutate(Model = "KDE-NB", Set = "Test",  Thr = round(thr_kde,3))
) %>% relocate(Model, Set, Thr)

kbl2(perf_kde_tuned, caption = "KDE-Naive Bayes with Youden-tuned threshold (chosen on training set)")

Model Set Thr AUC Sens Spec PPV NPV Acc

KDE-NB Test 0 0.9832041 0.9069767 0.9444444 0.9069767 0.9444444 0.9304348

Notes

  • KDE-NB drops the Normality assumption for continuous features; it can adapt to skewed or multi-modal FNA features.
  • We mix modeling choices: categorical features use smoothed class-conditional probabilities, continuous features use KDE — all multiplied under the Naive independence assumption.
  • Trade-offs: KDE adds flexibility but may overfit with tiny class-specific samples; bandwidth (bw, adjust) acts like a smoothness tuning parameter.

Part D — Gaussian Naive Bayes with cost

Here, we’ll repeat the Gaussian NB example except we’ll incorporate a cost function.

nb_gauss <- naiveBayes(Diagnosis ~ ., data = train, laplace = 0)  # no smoothing needed for continuous
# Posterior probability for Malignant ("M")
p_tr_g <- predict(nb_gauss, newdata = train, type = "raw")[,"M"]
p_te_g <- predict(nb_gauss, newdata = test,  type = "raw")[,"M"]

#### For screening, let's say a false negative (FN), saying a diseased person is healthy, 
#### is 10 times more costly than a false positive (FP), saying a healthy person is diseased.
#### When a FN is K times more costly, the natural threshold is 1/(K+1)
metrics_gauss_screen <- bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(train$Diagnosis, p_tr_g, thr = 1/11) %>% mutate(Set = "Train"),
  eval_metrics(test$Diagnosis,  p_te_g, thr = 1/11) %>% mutate(Set = "Test")
) %>% mutate(Type = "Screen", Threshold = 1/11) %>% relocate(Set,Type, Threshold)

#### For confirmation, let's say an FP is 10 times more costly than an FN.
#### When a FP is K times more costly, the natural threshold is K/(K+1)
metrics_gauss_confrm <- bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(train$Diagnosis, p_tr_g, thr = 10/11) %>% mutate(Set = "Train"),
  eval_metrics(test$Diagnosis,  p_te_g, thr = 10/11) %>% mutate(Set = "Test")
) %>% mutate(Type = "Confirm", Threshold = 10/11) %>% relocate(Set,Type, Threshold)

#### Overall
metrics_gauss <- metrics_gauss %>% 
  mutate(Type = "Overall", Threshold = 0.5) %>% relocate(Set,Type, Threshold)

#### Using a Youden-tuned threshold
thr_gauss <- tune_threshold_j(train$Diagnosis, p_tr_g)

metrics_gauss_tuned <- bind_rows(
  eval_metrics(train$Diagnosis, p_tr_g, thr_gauss) %>% mutate(Set = "Train"),
  eval_metrics(test$Diagnosis,  p_te_g, thr_gauss) %>% mutate(Set = "Test")
) %>% 
  mutate(Type = "Youden", Threshold = thr_gauss) %>% relocate(Set, Type, Threshold)

kbl2(metrics_gauss %>% 
       bind_rows(metrics_gauss_tuned) %>% 
       bind_rows(metrics_gauss_screen) %>% 
       bind_rows(metrics_gauss_confrm) %>% 
       filter(Set == "Test"), caption = "Gaussian Naive Bayes comparison for test set", digits = 3)
Gaussian Naive Bayes comparison for test set
Set Type Threshold AUC Sens Spec PPV NPV Acc
Test Overall 0.500 0.984 0.907 0.903 0.848 0.942 0.904
Test Youden 1.000 0.975 0.837 0.958 0.923 0.908 0.913
Test Screen 0.091 0.975 0.907 0.903 0.848 0.942 0.904
Test Confirm 0.909 0.975 0.907 0.903 0.848 0.942 0.904

For the confirmation method, we see an increase in Specificity, and PPV (as expected). What is surprising, is that we see an increase in NPV. This happens because while the confirmation method says 1 fewer person is sick, that person happens to be a healthy person. Normally, this will not be the case.

For the screening method, there is no increase sensitivity. The reason why this occurs is that no diseased individual has a predicted probability between 1/10 (the confirmation cutoff) and 10/11 (the screening cutoff). As a result, the screening cutoff does not result in additional true positives (TP) or fewer FNs.

par(c(2,1))
## NULL
hist(p_te_g[test$Diagnosis=="B"], breaks = 30, main = "Histogram of pi's for Healthy")

hist(p_te_g[test$Diagnosis=="M"], breaks = 30, main = "Histogram of pi's for Diseased")

Youden’s method ends up being what we would expect from a screening method.

Notes

  • For screening: decreasing the threshold will result in more FPs, less FNs, higher sensitivity, lower specificity, higher NPV, and lower PPV. The test will prioritize not missing diseased individuals, or ruling people out.
  • For confirmation: increasing the threshold will result in more FPs, less FNs, lower sensitivity, higher specificity, lower NPV, and higher PPV. The test will prioritize not saying healthy individuals are diseased.
  • For overall predictive accuracy: a threshold at 0.5 or chosen to maximize sensitivity + specificity (i.e., Youden’s J) is best.
